5.1 — The Axe: Item Pickups & Inventory Bools

Coins and potions changed numbers. The axe changes what you are. It flips a boolean — that half is easy, and you have written the pattern three times already — and then it replaces the entire machine that draws your character. Nothing you have built so far prepares you for the second half, and it is one line long.

In this lesson you will be able to answer“how do I add an item to my inventory?”Guided build
Break It Down~10 minGuided build

The player picks up an axe and becomes an axe-wielder — "how do I add an item to my inventory?" In a game where every pickup so far changed a number this game was keeping, and this one has to change the machine that draws the player.

First, before any code: cut that into parts small enough that you could look each one up on its own.

  1. Give the axe a shape the engine can report onA collider on the AxeItem prefab root with Is Trigger ticked, sized to the art — the recipe you followed for the coin in 2.1. The prefab already carries the Axe tag, and right now it has no collider at all, which makes it a picture you can walk straight through.Read: the Collider2D and Is Trigger rows in the quick reference, and the coin you gave a shape to in 2.1
  2. Put one where a player can reach itAn instance of the prefab standing in the Overworld. There are zero in any scene, so the mechanic is invisible until you place one — and it has to be somewhere a tester will walk without dying first.Read: the prefab-versus-instance distinction from 2.1, and the clone you spawned in 2.4 that showed you what a prefab owns
  3. Confirm the thing you touched was the axeelse if (other.CompareTag("Axe")) inside the OnTriggerEnter2D you already have. Your coin check from 2.1 and your potion check from 2.3 are already living in that method, so this is a third branch of an idea you have written twice.Read: the tag check you wrote in 2.1, and the other.CompareTag("Coin") row in the quick reference for the exact spelling
  4. Remember that you have itOne field in the class body — a bool that starts false and is set to true inside the branch. One item, one yes/no: there is no count because nobody has ever needed two axes.Read: the coin count field you declared in the class body in 2.1, and the bool hasAxe = false; row in the quick reference for the type
  5. write this partRead: the Animator component page in the Unity scripting reference — the property whose type is RuntimeAnimatorController — and the unused axe controller that is already sitting in Assets/Artwork/Animations/Top_Down/PlayerAnimator/Axe/
  6. Consume the pickupDestroy(other.gameObject) — the axe is an item you carry, so it leaves the world the moment you touch it, exactly like the coin and the potion. What stays behind is the boolean: the object is consumed, the capability is not.Read: the Destroy(gameObject) row in the quick reference, and the destroy line in your own coin branch

Five of those six parts are the pickup pattern you have now written three times: a shape, a tag check, a change, a destroy. Only one part has no precedent at all, and it is the reason this lesson exists. Every pickup so far changed a number the game was already keeping — a coin count, health. The boolean is that same shape wearing different clothes: a value that can only hold 0 or 1 is still a value. What is genuinely new is that the axe changes what the player is, and that is not done by changing a value at all — it is done by replacing the machine that decides which animation plays. Keeping those two jobs as separate parts is the whole point of the split: "remember the axe" and "become the axe-wielder" are different problems, and only one of them is new.

The test: could you look this part up on its own, right now, in one search? "Pick up an axe" cannot be looked up. "Change the controller an Animator is playing" can — and the search term for it is a property name you have to go and read rather than guess, which is why the gap above names where to look and not what to type.

Your turn

The axe flips a boolean that nothing in your game reads yet. Name one thing that will have to read it, and say what you expect that line of code to look like when something finally does.

Take the boolean away and keep only the swap; then take the swap away and keep only the boolean. Which of the two can the game not do without, and what does the other one buy you?

The Problem: A Pickup That Changes You ~15 min

Every pickup in this game so far has been easy to hold in your head, because it changed a number that already existed. Walk into a coin and coins goes up by one. Walk into a potion and health goes up. The axe does not do that. Walk into an axe and every number in your game stays exactly where it was — and the character you are controlling becomes somebody else.

So answer the data question before you build anything. Coins needed a counter. A potion needed to change an existing number. What does "the player is carrying an axe" actually need?

OptionWhat it storesWhy you would or would not
An int count How many axes you hold Useless extra information. Nobody has ever needed two axes, so you would be storing a number you will never read.
A bool Yes or no — you have one, or you do not The honest shape of the fact. One item, one yes/no, and the game only ever asks one question about it.
A list of items Every item you carry, by name The right answer for sixty items. Overkill for one, and it turns the simplest question in the game — "do I have an axe?" — into a search.
The boolean is the easy half, and it is the half that feels like the lesson. Everything this game has remembered so far has been a number that changes — a coin count, health, and the moment on the clock you kept on the turret. A bool is that same shape wearing different clothes: a value that can only ever be 0 or 1 is still a value, and you have declared one before. The half that has no precedent is what the axe does after the boolean flips: it decides which animation set the player is drawn with. Watch for it, because if you treat this lesson as "a pickup with a different tag", you will build half of it and not notice.
Go and look before you write a line. Open Assets/Prefabs/AxeItem and read the Inspector: a Transform, a Sprite Renderer, and the tag Axe. Now notice what is missing — and then count the axes placed in your scenes, because the answer is zero. The mechanic does not exist in the world yet; you are going to build it and then go and put it somewhere.

Then select the Sprite child under the Player and read the Animator component. It is playing Player_Shovel.controller — the state machine 1.6 taught you to drive. Now open Assets/Artwork/Animations/Top_Down/PlayerAnimator/ and count what is in there: two complete controllers, a shovel and an axe, and only one of them is referenced by anything in this project. Somebody built you the whole weapon set and left the second one on the shelf.

Socratic: Right-sizing the data

  1. Why is a bool the right abstraction for "I have an axe" but the wrong one for "how many coins do I have"?
  2. At roughly how many items does a collection of booleans become the wrong design? What breaks first — readability, or the number of branches you have to write?
  3. Where should this boolean live — on the axe, on the player, or somewhere global? Use the reasoning you applied in 2.1, then check it against what you actually do below.
Read the Docs: The API for Changing What You Are ~15 min

Six of the seven rows below are things you have already typed somewhere in this course, and the seventh is the one you are going to look up rather than guess. Read the cost column as carefully as the middle one — for the first time in this unit, the cost of the interesting row is what it does to the rest of the game, not what it does to a number.

APIWhat it gives youWhat it costs
bool True or false, one bit of information — the type you first met as isMoving in 1.6, now holding a fact about the player instead of a fact about the input. There is nothing in between. It cannot say how many and it cannot say how long — an int counts, a list holds many, and a bool is only ever the two answers. That is a feature exactly once per fact.
[SerializeField] private bool hasAxe = false; A class-body field that survives every frame and appears in the Inspector, so you can watch it flip while the game runs — the declaration form from 1.3 and the coin count from 2.1. The starting value is a design decision, not a formality. true and the capability is granted before the player has done anything; false and it is earned. The default is the difference between a reward and a decoration.
Collider2D ▸ Is Trigger ☑ ON The checkbox that changes what an overlap means: a trigger only reports that two shapes met, which is what makes OnTriggerEnter2D fire rather than OnCollisionEnter2D. A trigger pushes nothing. On a pickup that is exactly what you want; on the spike in 2.2 it was the bug — "it did not push me back" and "it did not notice me" look identical from the player's seat.
other.CompareTag("Axe") Asks the engine whether the collider you just touched carries that tag. The AxeItem prefab already has it, so there is nothing to create and no string to invent. Exact spelling against a tag that has to exist in the project, and it is asked of whichever object owns the collider — move the collider down to a child and the answer is false with nothing in the Console to explain it.
animator.SetBool / SetInteger / SetTrigger The three calls from 1.6 that make a controller play something: IsWalking, WalkDir, Attack. They choose between the states of one controller. None of them can reach a clip that is not in the machine you are currently playing — which is why a whole new weapon set is not a parameter, and never can be.
the Animator's own controller property The property on the Animator component that holds which controller it is playing right now. Read it and you know which weapon set is live; assign to it and the entire state machine — states, transitions, clips — is replaced in one line. Its type is RuntimeAnimatorController, which is the same type as the Inspector slot you wire. Find its name on the Animator component page of the Unity scripting reference rather than guessing it — the Socratic below asks you to, and the walkthrough leaves the line for you to write. It replaces everything: nothing you set on the old controller carries over, so the states and parameters you depend on have to exist in the new one (on this project they do — both controllers carry the same three parameters, which is why 1.6's code needs no edits). And nothing about the swap is saved: a Player rebuilt from the prefab comes back with the controller the prefab was wired with. SceneSwitch.cs exists partly because of that.
Destroy(Object) Removes the pickup's GameObject at the end of the frame — the line your coin and your potion already use. It is final, and it takes the object and not the capability. Destroying the axe does not un-set hasAxe: if the axe should ever be lost, some other code has to flip the boolean back, in the place where it is lost.
What the axe does not do. Notice what is missing from the walkthrough you are about to read: no Debug.Log in the pickup, no counter going up, no number changing anywhere. Collect the axe and the Console stays silent, because the axe is not feedback — it is a permission. A fact that future code will read before it allows an action. You are not building a score; you are building a capability, and the thing that proves it worked is that the character you are controlling looks different.

Socratic: Three ways to change a weapon

All three of these are legitimate. Read the cost column before you commit:

ApproachHow it worksWhat it costs
Assign the other controller at runtime The Animator component has a property holding the controller it is currently playing. Hand it the axe controller when the axe is picked up and the whole state machine — states, transitions, clips — is replaced instantly. Nothing to author, and it works for any weapon set somebody else has already built. You must remember to set it back if the axe is ever lost, and nothing about it survives a scene load unless something puts it back.
Author the axe states into one controller Add the axe states and transitions into the controller you already have, and drive them with a new parameter. You duplicate an entire state machine by hand, and every future clip has to be added twice. It also means editing an asset somebody else built for you.
Use an Animator Override Controller A Unity asset built for exactly this: it takes one base controller and swaps the clips it plays, keeping all the logic in one place. One extra asset to create, and one more concept to learn before you can build anything. This is the professional answer, and it is not today's answer.
  1. Which approach does the project's own art layout clearly intend you to take? What is the evidence?
  2. Read Assets/Scripts/Package Scripts/SceneSwitch.cs. Find where it saves and restores something related to the Animator. Which property does it touch, and what does that prove is possible at runtime?
  3. Which approach would you choose if this game had four weapons instead of two, and why does the answer change?
Build It With MeGuided build

The question this answers“how do I add an item to my inventory?”

You are editing Assets/Scripts/PlayerController.cs. Two new fields, one new branch inside the pickup callback you already have, and one assignment that replaces the machine drawing your character. The shape is the coin pickup from 2.1 with a different tag; the last line of step 3 is the part nothing before it prepares you for.

This build leaves 1 line for you to write. Everything around it is given, so you always know the shape of what you are producing.

Step 1Make the axe a pickup — this step is not code

The AxeItem prefab is a picture with a tag on it, and there is not one axe placed in any scene. Nothing you write in the rest of this lesson can fire until both of those change.

// Assets/Prefabs/AxeItem ▸ the Inspector

Box Collider 2D   ▸ added to the ROOT, sized by hand
Box Collider 2D   ▸ Is Trigger   ☑ ON

// Overworld ▸ drag one AxeItem from Assets/Prefabs into the scene
  1. 1Open the prefab asset in Assets/Prefabs, not an instance in the scene. Read the Inspector: a Transform, a Sprite Renderer, and the tag Axe already set. Then notice what is missing — every other pickup in this game has one, and this one does not.
  2. 3Add the collider to the root — the object carrying the Axe tag — then drag its handles in the Scene view until the green outline covers the axe you can actually see. The axe sprite is a wide, short shape rather than a round one, so a Box fits it more easily than the coin's Circle did in 2.1.The root, not a child. CompareTag is asked of whichever object owns the collider, and the root is the object tagged Axe. This is the same trap as the coin in 2.1, and it fails the same silent way: the overlap never reports, and nothing in the Console says why.
  3. 4Tick it. A trigger reports an overlap and pushes nothing — the checkbox you met on the coin, and the one that decides which callback fires.This is the difference between a pickup and a wall. Leave it off and the axe becomes a small solid obstacle: it shoves the player aside, it never leaves the ground, and OnTriggerEnter2D never runs at all. You would get OnCollisionEnter2D instead — the callback you met on the spike in 2.2 — and the axe would just sit there being a rock.
  4. 6There are zero axe instances in any scene, so nothing is a pickup until you place one. Put it somewhere a tester will walk into it without being killed first; the route toward a cave mouth is the sensible place, because 5.2 is where that door starts caring whether you have it.

Step 2Declare the state, and the controller you will become

Two lines in the class body, next to your coin count and your health. One of them is what this lesson is about; the other is a reference to an asset that is not wired to anything in the project yet.

    [SerializeField] private bool hasAxe = false;

    [SerializeField] private RuntimeAnimatorController axeController;
  1. 1The capability. A bool holds true or false and nothing else, which is the honest shape of "I have an axe": one item, one yes/no. There is no count because nobody has ever needed two axes — the int that serves your coins would be storing a number you would never read.Get the starting value the right way round. false means you do not have the axe until you find it. Start it true and the game has granted you the capability before you have walked anywhere — and because your character already looks like an axe-wielder, the pickup appears to do nothing at all — the Build Lab asks you to say exactly what the player gets for free if you pick that value.
  2. 3A slot in the Inspector that will hold the controller asset for the axe. Leave it empty for now — step 4 wires it from the Project window. This is the [SerializeField] slot pattern from 1.3, the same one that holds your speed and your coin count.A slot rather than a typed-in path. The controller is an asset sitting in Assets/Artwork/Animations/Top_Down/PlayerAnimator/Axe/, and a field wired in the Inspector is a reference to that asset: rename it, move it, and the reference survives. A string path typed into your code would break the moment anybody tidied the folder.

Step 3Add the axe to the callback that already handles pickups

One more branch inside the OnTriggerEnter2D you have had since 2.1. The coin check stays exactly where it is; the axe is one more question asked of the same event.

    private void OnTriggerEnter2D(Collider2D other)
    {
        if (other.CompareTag("Coin"))
        {
            coins = coins + 1;
            Destroy(other.gameObject);
        }
        else if (other.CompareTag("Axe"))
        {
            hasAxe = true;
            animator.____ = ____;
            Destroy(other.gameObject);
        }
    }
  1. 8The new question. The prefab has carried the tag Axe since the day you opened it, so there is nothing to create and nothing to spell-check — but it is still CompareTag and not ==, for the reason from 2.1.else if rather than a second if, so each object is asked exactly one question. No collider is a coin and an axe at once, so it makes no difference to the game — it says what you mean: one overlap, one answer.
  2. 10Sets the capability. No type in front of it: the field already exists in the class body, so this assigns to it — the declare-versus-assign rule from 1.3. Declaring it here instead would build a brand-new bool, throw it away at the end of the frame, and leave the real one false forever.
  3. Your turn11The last line of the pickup, and the whole of "becoming an axe-wielder". The line above says that you have the axe; this one is what puts it in your hands, by handing the Animator a different controller to play. Keep the receiver exactly as written — animator is the field you cached in 1.6, and it is the same Animator that has been playing your shovel. The right-hand side is the slot you declared in step 2.You want the property on animator that holds which controller it is playing right now — the same type as the slot you declared, so the two sides of this assignment are the same kind of thing. The Animator component page in the Unity scripting reference lists it among its properties; it is the one whose type is RuntimeAnimatorController.Nothing else in this file changes when you pick up the axe — your movement, your input, your health and the coin branch above are all exactly what they were, and the three parameters from 1.6 (IsWalking, WalkDir, Attack) keep driving the new controller without a single edit. That is the surprise: the player does not transition into being an axe-wielder, the machine that draws the player is replaced. And because it is replaced rather than saved, it is gone the moment a fresh Player is built from the prefab — which is exactly why SceneSwitch.cs saves the controller before it loads a scene and puts it back in Start(). The Build Lab asks you to explain why that code has to exist.
  4. 12The axe leaves the world the moment you pick it up — the same line as the coin and the potion. What stays behind is the boolean: the object is consumed, the capability is not.

Step 4Wire the slot, then prove it is real state

The swap does nothing until the Inspector slot holds a controller. Then find out whether the boolean you wrote is genuinely state, or a value that forgets itself.

  1. 1Select the Player prefab, find the slot you declared in step 2, and drag Axe/Player_Axe.controller from the Project window into it. Wire it on the prefab, not on one Player in a scene, so every Player you ever place inherits it.Leave this slot at None and you hand the Animator an empty controller the moment you touch the axe: the boolean flips, and the character does not change — and because the Animator now has nothing to play, no swing plays at all. Nothing in the Console points at the line that did it.
  2. 2Add Debug.Log("Has axe: " + hasAxe); to Update() for one run. Watch the Console repeat false while you walk around, walk into the axe, and watch it flip to true and stay there. Then delete the print — the proof is the behaviour, not the message, and a log in Update() runs sixty times a second forever.
  3. 3Save, press Play, walk into the axe and click. The character you are controlling should be an axe-wielder now: new walk, new idle, an axe swing instead of a shovel. Nothing else about the player changed — you can still move, still take damage, still collect coins.
  4. 4The axe should still be in your hands, because SceneSwitch.cs copies the controller off the Player before it loads the scene and hands it back in Start(). Read that method now, while the behaviour is fresh — it is your proof that a controller can be swapped at runtime at all, and it is the code you will be glad existed in 5.3.
Check your work: the finished filetry every gap first — then open this to compare

Compare against your own file rather than copying it. Two differences are worth naming, because neither is a mistake. First the shape: this file chains else if in the walkthrough and returns early out of each branch here — both ask every object exactly one question, and any form that ends up setting the boolean and swapping the controller is correct. Second the helper: here the swap lives in a small method called PickUpAxe(), and the walkthrough writes the same two lines inline — the method is there so that "becoming an axe-wielder" has a name you can point at. What is NOT a difference is the gap itself: whichever way you wrote it, the line that changes the player is the assignment to the Animator's controller property, and that name is the one you had to go and read.

// ------------------------------------------------------------------
//  REFERENCE FILE — Assets/Scripts/PlayerController.cs
//  Written to be read, not pasted. Build it with the walkthrough
//  above, one step at a time, then open this and compare.
//  If it is sitting in your project unchanged, that is the thing
//  to go and do now — the walkthrough is still above you.
// ------------------------------------------------------------------
using UnityEngine;

// Your controller at the end of 5.1: movement and health from 2.2, animation
// from 1.6, the coin pickup from 2.1 — and the axe.
public class PlayerController : MonoBehaviour
{
    [SerializeField] private float moveSpeed = 5f;
    [SerializeField] private int health = 3;
    [SerializeField] private int coins;

    // The capability, and the controller that draws it. The starting value is
    // the design: false, until the player earns it.
    [SerializeField] private bool hasAxe = false;
    [SerializeField] private RuntimeAnimatorController axeController;

    private Rigidbody2D body;
    private Animator animator;
    private SpriteRenderer spriteRenderer;

    private float inputX;
    private float inputY;

    void Start()
    {
        // Looked up once, never inside Update() — the rules from 1.6 and 2.2.
        body = GetComponent<Rigidbody2D>();
        animator = GetComponentInChildren<Animator>();
        spriteRenderer = GetComponentInChildren<SpriteRenderer>();
    }

    void Update()
    {
        inputX = Input.GetAxis("Horizontal");
        inputY = Input.GetAxis("Vertical");

        Vector2 direction = new Vector2(inputX, inputY);

        // No Time.deltaTime: velocity is per second, not per frame.
        body.linearVelocity = direction * moveSpeed;

        UpdateAnimation();
        CheckAttack();
    }

    void UpdateAnimation()
    {
        bool isMoving = inputX != 0f || inputY != 0f;
        animator.SetBool("IsWalking", isMoving);

        if (Mathf.Abs(inputX) >= Mathf.Abs(inputY))
        {
            animator.SetInteger("WalkDir", 1);
            spriteRenderer.flipX = inputX < 0f;
        }
        else if (inputY > 0f)
        {
            animator.SetInteger("WalkDir", 0);
        }
        else
        {
            animator.SetInteger("WalkDir", 2);
        }
    }

    void CheckAttack()
    {
        if (Input.GetMouseButtonDown(0))
        {
            animator.SetTrigger("Attack");
        }
    }

    private void OnCollisionEnter2D(Collision2D collision)
    {
        if (collision.gameObject.CompareTag("Spikes"))
        {
            TakeDamage(1);
        }
    }

    // Every pickup in the game arrives here. The axe is one more question.
    // Your potion branch from 2.3 lives in this same callback, under its own
    // tag — it is left out here only because the tag is the one you invented.
    private void OnTriggerEnter2D(Collider2D other)
    {
        if (other.CompareTag("Coin"))
        {
            coins = coins + 1;
            Destroy(other.gameObject);
            return;
        }

        if (other.CompareTag("Axe"))
        {
            PickUpAxe();
            Destroy(other.gameObject);
        }
    }

    // The whole of "becoming an axe-wielder", and the only line in the game
    // that changes what the player IS. Setting a parameter picks a clip inside
    // one controller; this replaces the whole controller — every state, every
    // transition, every clip, in one assignment. Swap the slot in the Inspector
    // and nothing here changes; that is the point.
    private void PickUpAxe()
    {
        hasAxe = true;
        animator.runtimeAnimatorController = axeController;
    }

    private void TakeDamage(int amount)
    {
        if (health <= 0)
        {
            return;
        }

        health = health - amount;
        Debug.Log("Health: " + health);

        if (health <= 0)
        {
            Debug.Log("Player died.");
        }
    }
}

// Inspector, on Assets/Prefabs/AxeItem:
//   Tag              =  Axe          <- already on the prefab; do not retype it
//   Box Collider 2D  =  on the ROOT, Is Trigger ON, sized to the art
//
// Inspector, on Assets/Prefabs/Player ▸ PlayerController:
//   Has Axe          =  off          <- earned in OnTriggerEnter2D, never granted
//   Axe Controller   =  Player_Axe   <- Assets/Artwork/Animations/Top_Down/
//                                       PlayerAnimator/Axe/Player_Axe.controller
//
// One axe instance must be standing in the Overworld. The prefab ships with
// zero instances in any scene, and nothing is a pickup until one is placed.
Build Lab: Put the Axe in the World ~25 min

Step 1 — prove the boolean is state, not a message. The walkthrough had you print hasAxe every frame and then delete the print. Do it in that order, and watch the Console while you do: a value that reads false for as long as you walk around and true from the moment you touch the axe is a value that remembers. Then delete it — Update() runs sixty times a second, and a print that survives into next lesson is noise you will be reading past.

Step 2 — decide where the axe lives. There were zero axe instances in any scene when you started, and you placed at least one. Now defend the placement like a level designer: which route does the player take to reach it, and what do they meet on the way? An axe nobody can find is the same as no axe at all, and no compiler will ever tell you.

Step 3 — decide what the axe means. The boolean now exists and nothing in your game reads it. That is the correct state for this lesson and the wrong state for the next one — 5.2 is where a door starts caring. Write down, before you finish, the one piece of future code you are most confident will read this field.

Architectural specification for PlayerController.cs:

The pickup — getting it into the world:

  • The AxeItem prefab carries the tag Axe and nothing else. What is it missing that every other pickup in this game has, and which object does it go on?
  • Trigger or solid — and what is your reason? What exactly would you see and hear if you chose the other one?
  • You added a collider to an object that has never had one, which means you cannot see what the engine sees. How did you check the shape in the Scene view rather than guessing, and what does it cost the player if the box is twice the size of the art?
  • The prefab ships with zero instances in any scene. Where did you place yours, and how would a tester find it without being told?

The state — one field, and the whole lesson hangs off it:

  • What type is the field, and why is that the right amount of information rather than an int or a list? Use the table at the top of the lesson.
  • What value does it start at, and what does the player get for free if you pick the other one? Answer in one sentence about their first five seconds of play.
  • Where does the field live, and what breaks if you get that wrong? Use the word "frame" in your answer.
  • Nothing in your game reads this field yet. Name one thing that will, and say what you expect that line of code to look like.

The swap — the new mechanism:

  • Which property on the Animator holds the controller it is currently playing, and where did you read that rather than guess it?
  • What did you have to do in the Inspector before the swap could work at all — and what does the player see if you skip it?
  • The three parameters from 1.6 — IsWalking, WalkDir, Attack — exist on both controllers with the same names and the same types. What does that tell you about how much of your 1.6 code had to change when the axe arrived?
  • The swap is one assignment and it is not saved anywhere. What puts it back when a scene loads, and why does that code have to exist?
  • The axe is one-use: breaking the door in 5.2 consumes it. What has to happen to the controller at that moment, which script should do it, and why must it not be the pickup branch?

Save and press Play. Walk into the axe and swing — the character should visibly become someone else the moment you touch it, and stay that way. Then walk through a cave mouth and come back, and check that they still are.

You have a mechanic that works and a design that is still entirely yours. These four questions are about the design half — and the first one is a look at what this project does not have, which tells you something about how the person who built it expected weapons to be added.

Checkpoint — before moving on, you must be able to:

  • Explain when a bool fits a fact and when it does not, and right-size the data for a new pickup
  • Build an item that grants capability instead of changing a number — trigger collider, tag check, default value and all
  • Compare the three ways to change a weapon set, and defend your choice
